label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
Peter, I respect the payroll experience behind your advice, and I agree that an informal scheme can get out of hand. If people are taking an advance every month, that deserves attention. Leavers can leave a balance behind, and the time spent approving requests is a real cost. Brenda’s Finance Manager is right to ask about cash flow too.

Where I disagree is the idea that people necessarily adjust after a couple of pay cycles, or that the consequences of their borrowing elsewhere stay outside the company. We tried almost exactly the approach you suggest and ended up reversing it.

I’m in HR at a logistics business with about 340 staff across Embakasi and Changamwe. A lot of our people are drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. In February 2025, after Finance raised much the same objections, we closed our informal advance scheme. We gave two months’ notice and arranged a financial literacy session with the SACCO.

The notice and the session were worth doing. But they didn’t make the emergencies disappear.

In the six months after we closed the scheme, calls to the office from debt collectors and loan apps went from a handful to **61 logged by reception**. Some apps were calling supervisors whom employees had listed as “referees”. So while the loan contract was the employee’s own, dealing with the calls became a workplace issue.

We also saw unplanned absence rise in the two days after month-end. Our Fleet Manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers taking time to sort out loans. I can’t say closing advances caused every call or absence, and I wouldn’t pretend we calculated the full cost of those missed runs. But it was enough to challenge our assumption that closing the window had made the problem go away.

One case that stayed with me was a loader at Changamwe who came to me with six loan apps running at once. He was borrowing from one to pay another. It took us four months, working with payroll, to unwind it. That is HR and payroll time too, even if it doesn’t show up in the advance administration line.

On SACCOs: I’m a supporter, but ours take two to three weeks to process a loan and require guarantors. That’s not much help when a child is sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. Financial literacy matters as well, but knowing how to budget doesn’t necessarily create emergency money for someone earning KES 28,000 a month.

We reopened advances in September 2025, but **not on the old informal terms**. We put the rules in writing:

- A maximum of **40% of net pay**.
- One request per pay cycle.
- Repaid in full at the next payroll, with no fee.
- Requests through the payroll portal, rather than someone having to come and explain themselves in my office.
- A check on total deductions before approval. The Employment Act limits deductions to two-thirds of wages, and we check that limit alongside the advance so nobody is left with nothing at month-end.

Since reopening, we’ve had roughly 55–70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. We’ve recovered everything except balances from two leavers, with roughly KES 14,000 written off for the year. Peter is right that leavers are a risk; that is our actual experience, not a reason to pretend the risk doesn’t exist.

The repeat requests also deserve watching. A once-per-cycle limit doesn’t, by itself, stop someone relying on an advance every month. We shouldn’t present a policy as a cure for financial pressure, and I’d still want to know whether particular employees need support beyond another advance.

What changed Finance’s view was that the scheme is now visible and bounded. Our Finance Manager actually defends it himself now because he can forecast against a known ceiling instead of discovering informal payments after the fact. That doesn’t mean there’s no cash-flow impact; it means there’s a defined limit to plan around.

Brenda, for your meeting on the 18th, I’d suggest going in with a comparison rather than arguing that advances cost nothing. Ask Finance to put a figure on administration time, forecast impact and likely write-offs. Then bring in what you can find on absence, disruption to production, collection calls and staff time spent dealing with the fallout. Some of those costs sit with supervisors, reception or operations rather than Finance, which can make them easy to miss. If you don’t have reliable figures yet, say so rather than guessing.

You could propose a written policy as an alternative to either the current informal arrangement or a complete shutdown: a net-pay cap, one request per pay cycle, full repayment at the next payroll, a clear payroll approval route and a deductions check. The exact cap would need to work for your workforce and cash flow; 40% is what we use, not a magic number. You could also agree with Finance on what to track and when to review it, including repeat requests and leavers’ balances.

Peter, I’m not arguing that an employer should become a bank or that every advance request should be approved. I am saying that closing an informal scheme isn’t the only way to get control of it. In our case, a limited, written scheme gave Finance more certainty and kept some very expensive problems from landing elsewhere in the business.
